failure_summary.description: 'The Highland version of this instrument': the agent answered the modified variant from the passages ('Great Highland Bagpipe'), which repeats the clue's modifier. The generic parent noun in its standard plural form ('Bagpipes') was wanted, and the existing 'Modifier version of this' rule was not applied.

A bare catchphrase or exclamation ('Yabba Dabba Do!') was answered with a passage title that merely contains the phrase ('I Yabba-Dabba Do!'). The skill covers lists of catchphrases but not a single one, so the show or character it belongs to ('The Flintstones') was missed.

patch.reasoning: Both failures echoed words from the clue and ignored the referent. In one case the agent returned a title or variant that contains the clue's words instead of the parent entity (a show for a catchphrase, a generic instrument for a regional variant). The edits add a rule for a lone catchphrase, an extension of the existing modifier-version rule to variant names found in passages, and a narrow note that standard plural names keep the plural. These patch gaps without duplicating existing rules or loosening the singular default for ordinary nouns.

edits.target: If the list is of real people, answer with the team, state or other entity they share.
edits.content: - A clue that is just ONE catchphrase, exclamation, slogan or line of dialogue with no 'this ...' pointer ('"Yabba Dabba Do!"', '"D'oh!"', '"Eureka!"') asks for the SOURCE it belongs to: the TV series, film, character or speaker the passages tie it to ('The Flintstones'). Passages are full of titles that merely contain the phrase ('I Yabba-Dabba Do!' is a TV movie, a spin-off of the series). Never echo the quote or a title built from its words. Apply the delete-clue-words test: if your answer contains the clue's words, step up to the parent franchise, series or person. Keep a leading 'The' when it is part of the show's standard title.

edits.target: Other clue details (diet, ingredient, cooking method) are just conditions on the generic dish.
edits.content: - The same holds when the modifier is a region, nationality or variant adjective and the noun is generic ('The Highland version of this instrument has a blowpipe, a chanter & 3 drones' -> 'Bagpipes'; 'the Bengal type of this animal' -> 'Tiger'). Passages are titled with the specific variant ('Great Highland Bagpipe'), but that variant contains the clue's own modifier. The answer is the PARENT thing the variant is a version of, as the general article title gives it ('Bagpipes - Wikipedia').

- Some things have a plural standard name (bagpipes, scissors, pliers, trousers, glasses, bellows, Flintstones-style series titles). Keep the plural form that the general article or passage titles use ('Bagpipes'), not a made-up singular ('Bagpipe').
